short: The staff officer who argued the tank into existence and wrote the first tank tactics.
full:
Ernest Swinton was a Royal Engineer who spent the first months of the war on the Western Front as Eyewitness, the only officially accredited British correspondent, writing censored dispatches for the press. What he saw of machine guns and wire led him in October 1914 to press Maurice Hankey, secretary of the Committee of Imperial Defence, for an armoured tracked machine built on the American Holt tractor. The War Office was unmoved; the Admiralty's Landships Committee was not, and Swinton later drafted the performance specification the rhomboid design was built to meet.

In February 1916 he wrote Notes on the Employment of Tanks, the first tactical doctrine for armour, which argued for mass, surprise and close infantry co-operation — advice ignored on the Somme and vindicated at Cambrai. He commanded the Heavy Section, Machine Gun Corps during its formation but was removed before it saw action. The Royal Commission on Awards to Inventors credited the machine itself to Tritton and Wilson. Swinton was Chichele Professor of Military History at Oxford from 1925 to 1939.
